summary: 14-day analysis of AAPS closed-loop data with 98.7% CGM coverage. Overall TIR 86.0%, TAR 8.9%, TBR 5.1%, CV 32.6%. Zero carbohydrate entries were recorded across the period. All meal coverage is handled reactively by UAM detection driving SMB and temp basal delivery. This creates a consistent cycle: unannounced meals produce daytime hyperglycemia (TAR 20-32% between 09:00-16:00), UAM responds with delayed insulin, and stacked IOB from corrections contributes to overnight hypoglycemia (TBR 10-18% at 00:00-02:00) and afternoon crashes (TBR 7.7-15.3% at 17:00-19:00). Basal rates appear approximately appropriate for fasting periods. GLP-1 doses (1.25mg on Aug 14, 17, 20) amplify insulin sensitivity and correlate with severe hypoglycemic events. The primary intervention is introducing carbohydrate entries with meal boluses to break the reactive hyperglycemia-overcorrection cycle.

analysis_steps.findings: CGM coverage is 98.7% with 3,995 valid entries and 10 gaps (largest 65 minutes). Estimated cadence is 5 minutes. No invalid or duplicate entries. AAPS profile is complete with all basal, CR, ISF, target, DIA, and SMB/UAM/automation settings present. Zero carbohydrate entries exist across the entire 14-day period. Three GLP-1 doses recorded as notes but not as structured treatments. Data quality is sufficient for hourly and daily pattern analysis.
analysis_steps.evidence: 3,995 valid entries out of 4,046 expected. 10 gaps, largest 65 minutes. 2,315 treatments including 655 insulin entries and 0 carb entries. 24 therapy response windows extracted. 27 events including GLP-1 notes, site changes, sensor changes, and profile switches.
analysis_steps.data_gaps: No carbohydrate entries prevent CR and meal bolus validation. GLP-1 timing exists as notes but dosage effect cannot be quantified from telemetry alone.

analysis_steps.findings: Overall mean glucose 121.6 mg/dL, SD 39.7, CV 32.6%. TIR 86.0%, TAR 8.9%, TBR 5.1%. Hypoglycemia concentrated in overnight hours (00:00-02:00 local, TBR 10-18.5%) and late afternoon/early evening (17:00-19:00, TBR 7.7-15.3%). Hyperglycemia clusters midday to afternoon (09:00-16:00, TAR up to 32.1%). Eight glucose extremes below 55 mg/dL, lowest 41 mg/dL. Eight extremes above 250 mg/dL, highest 293 mg/dL. CV of 32.6% indicates significant variability driven by unannounced meals and reactive corrections. Two pump error/occlusion events noted on Aug 19. One severe crash from 172 to 42 mg/dL on Aug 13 within 4 hours of a 0.2U correction bolus.
analysis_steps.evidence: Hourly glucose patterns show TBR peaks at 01:00 (18.5%) and 19:00 (15.3%). TAR peaks at 16:00 (32.1%). Daily extremes include Aug 10 (TBR 6.9%, TAR 13.0%), Aug 14 (TAR 20.8%, TBR 8.3%), Aug 18 (TBR 12.8%, TAR 15.3%). Glucose extremes: 41 mg/dL (Aug 14), 42 mg/dL (Aug 13, Aug 21), 293 mg/dL (Aug 15).
analysis_steps.data_gaps: No activity or exercise annotations to contextualize hypoglycemia events. No carb records to separate meal-driven from basal-driven excursions.

analysis_steps.findings: Seven basal segments (0.5-0.8 U/h) and three target segments (90-100 mg/dL) are configured. Overnight (00:00-04:00, basal 0.6 U/h): average glucose 93-105 mg/dL near the 90 mg/dL target, but TBR 10-18.5% in the first two hours of the night. TBR drops to 3-4.8% by 02:00-06:00, suggesting the overnight lows are driven by residual IOB from daytime corrections rather than excessive basal rate. Dawn transition (05:00-08:00, basal 0.7-0.8): glucose stable with TBR below 5%, basal step-up appears appropriate. Daytime (09:00-16:00, basal 0.7-0.8): glucose rises from 133 to 163 mg/dL with TAR reaching 32%, but this window coincides with unannounced meal timing and cannot be attributed to basal deficit without fasting data. Afternoon (16:00-19:00, basal 0.5-0.6): glucose falls sharply from 163 to 124 mg/dL despite the lowest basal rate, with TBR rising to 15.3%. The 0.5 U/h segment is likely appropriate as a floor; crashes are driven by correction bolus stacking on falling postprandial glucose. Evening (19:00-00:00, basal 0.6-0.7): glucose rises to 120-128 then drifts to 106 by 23:00. Basal rates are approximately correct for the observed patterns; the primary dysregulation is from unannounced meals and IOB stacking.
analysis_steps.data_gaps: No fasting windows can be isolated without carb records. No structured exercise annotations. Meal timing inferred from glucose patterns only.

analysis_steps.findings: ISF is a single segment of 56 mg/dL/U for all 24 hours. Correction-only therapy response windows show highly variable effectiveness: some corrections produce drops consistent with or exceeding 56 mg/dL/U while others show inadequate response when meals are suspected. Dynamic ISF (enabled, 70% adjustment factor) and GLP-1 co-administration create wide effective ISF variation (observed range 27.8-124 mg/dL/U). The Aug 13 crash (172 to 42 mg/dL on 0.2U) and Aug 14 crash (234 to 56 mg/dL on 0.2U) indicate periods of profound insulin sensitivity where the static ISF is too weak. DIA of 10 hours means IOB from afternoon corrections persists into overnight hours, consistent with the overnight hypoglycemia pattern. CR has 5 segments (13, 11.1, 13.2, 10.5, 12.6 g/U) that are structurally reasonable but cannot be validated because zero carb entries exist. The 10.5 g/U at 16:00-20:00 is the most aggressive segment, aligning with observed afternoon insulin sensitivity.
analysis_steps.evidence: 24 therapy response windows, all correction boluses. Key events: Aug 10 01:56 (141 to 99 on 0.2U, effective ~210 mg/dL/U), Aug 11 15:51 (165 to 98 on 0.2U, effective ~335 mg/dL/U), Aug 13 13:05 (172 to 47 on 0.2U, effective ~625 mg/dL/U), Aug 14 16:20 (234 to 56 on 0.2U, effective ~890 mg/dL/U). Dynamic ISF variable_sens range: 27.8 to 124 mg/dL/U. GLP-1 doses on Aug 14, 17, 20. CR segments: 00:00=13, 04:00=11.1, 08:00=13.2, 16:00=10.5, 20:00=12.6 g/U.
analysis_steps.data_gaps: No carb-bolus pairs to validate CR. No structured fasting windows with known ISF verification. GLP-1 dose-response relationship unknown. U200 insulin pharmacokinetics may differ from standard models.

analysis_steps.findings: UAM is the sole meal-response mechanism because zero carb entries exist. UAM detection creates COB and triggers SMB and temp basal delivery, but with an inherent 15-30+ minute lag behind meal absorption. This reactive design explains the daytime hyperglycemia pattern. UAM-driven insulin can overshoot when actual meal absorption is faster than modeled COB decay, contributing to the afternoon crash pattern. SMB fires at 3-minute intervals with 15-20 minute basal equivalents. SMB continues during user-set temp targets (smb_with_temp_target_enabled=true), which is a material safety concern: six temp targets of 135 mg/dL were set across the period, likely for activity, yet SMB continued delivering insulin during these windows. The Aug 15 temp target event shows glucose falling from 174 to 66 mg/dL during a period when the user explicitly requested reduced insulin. SMB frequency and strength settings are appropriate for the no-bolus context.
analysis_steps.evidence: Loop logs show UAM Boost values from 0.44 to 35.93. SMB microboluses of 0.05-0.4U at 3-minute intervals. Temp targets set on Aug 9, 15, 17, 18, 19, 20, all at 135 mg/dL. Aug 15 temp target at 13:24 (BG 174) followed by drop to 66 by 15:30. UAM Boost 2 reached 35.93 on Aug 13 preceding the crash to 42 mg/dL. SMB activation: smb_always_enabled=true, smb_with_temp_target_enabled=true.
analysis_steps.data_gaps: No activity or exercise annotations to confirm temp target context. UAM COB decay curves not available in telemetry.

analysis_steps.findings: Dynamic ISF is enabled with a 70% adjustment factor, producing effective ISF values from 27.8 to 124 mg/dL/U from a profile base of 56 mg/dL/U. Autosens is disabled. Dynamic ISF compensates for the single-segment ISF profile but is reactive rather than predictive, creating a lag between actual sensitivity changes and detection. This lag allows insulin delivery based on a stale ISF during periods of rapidly increasing sensitivity, contributing to overcorrection crashes. The 70% adjustment factor allows ISF to drop to approximately 30% of profile, which amplifies correction doses during GLP-1-enhanced sensitivity periods. Max basal (12 U/h) and max IOB (25 U) are non-binding safety backstops that do not constrain observed behavior. The sensitivity_ratio of approximately 1.0 is the Dynamic ISF neutral state, not a disabled indicator. Dynamic ISF is compensating for the absence of time-segmented ISF, but this compensation is inherently reactive and contributes to the hyperglycemia-overcorrection cycle.
analysis_steps.evidence: Observed variable_sens range: 27.8 (Aug 21, BG 245) to 124.0 (Aug 11, post-sensor change). Crash events: Aug 13 variable_sens=53.4, Aug 14 variable_sens=42.5 (GLP-1 day), Aug 19 variable_sens=37.9. Highest observed temp basal: 3.6 U/h. Highest observed IOB: 5.935 U. Dynamic ISF adjustment factor: 70%. Autosens disabled. sensitivity_ratio range: 0.94-1.0.
analysis_steps.data_gaps: No fasting basal tests to independently verify ISF by time of day. GLP-1 dose-response curve unknown. U200 insulin pharmacokinetics may differ from standard models used by Dynamic ISF.

analysis_steps.findings: No meal bolus strategy exists. Zero carbohydrate entries across 14 days. The user-declared analysis_context has empty meal_strategies. All meal coverage is reactive UAM. Hourly glucose patterns reveal clear meal-driven excursions: breakfast (07:00-09:00, rise from 99.5 to 132.9), lunch (12:00-14:00, peak to 148.1, TAR 26.3%), and possible evening meal (20:00-22:00, rise from 117 to 127.6). The absence of meal boluses is the root cause of the primary dysregulation cycle: unannounced meals produce hyperglycemia, UAM responds with delayed insulin, and stacked IOB causes subsequent hypoglycemia. The existing CR profile (13.2 g/U daytime, 10.5 g/U evening) is structurally reasonable but unvalidated. SMB cannot substitute for a pre-meal bolus because its delivery onset is 15-30 minutes behind the meal even with UAM active. Introducing carb entries with immediate boluses would reduce hyperglycemia peaks and the subsequent IOB stacking that drives overnight and afternoon hypoglycemia.
analysis_steps.evidence: Hourly glucose shows meal-correlated rises: 07:00-09:00 (99.5 to 132.9), 09:00-12:00 (132.9 to 141.3), 12:00-14:00 (141.3 to 148.1, TAR 14 to 26.3%), 20:00-22:00 (117 to 127.6). Zero carb entries in treatment_summary and carb_treatment_entries. All 24 therapy response windows are correction boluses with is_extended_carbs=false. CR segments: 08:00-16:00=13.2, 16:00-20:00=10.5, 20:00-00:00=12.6 g/U. analysis_context.meal_strategies is empty.
analysis_steps.data_gaps: No carb entries of any kind prevent CR validation, prebolus timing assessment, and bolus adequacy evaluation. The single observation that would improve confidence most is one week of carb entries for at least two meals per day using the existing CR of 13.2 g/U.

analysis_steps.findings: No extended carbohydrate entries exist across the 14-day period. Zero e-carb entries, zero extended boluses, and zero meal announcements. The meal_max_absorption_hours of 7 hours is the UAM absorption ceiling, not an e-carb setting. E-carbs are not applicable in the current workflow because the user must first establish basic carb entries and meal boluses before considering e-carbs for extended-absorption meals. The 7-hour meal_max_absorption_hours may extend UAM-modeled COB beyond actual meal duration, contributing to phantom IOB that can suppress insulin delivery when actual meal absorption is complete.
analysis_steps.evidence: carb_treatment_entries is empty. treatment_summary.extended_carb_entries=0. treatment_summary.average_extended_carb_duration_min=null. All 24 therapy_response_windows have is_extended_carbs=false. No e-carb entries in representative_treatments. meal_max_absorption_hours=7 from aaps_profile.smb_settings.raw_settings.
analysis_steps.data_gaps: None for the negative finding. E-carbs cannot be evaluated until carb entries are established.

analysis_steps.findings: The primary dysregulation pattern is driven by the absence of carbohydrate entries. All meal coverage is reactive UAM, creating a consistent cycle of hyperglycemia → delayed insulin → IOB stacking → hypoglycemia. Three competing explanations for overnight hypoglycemia were resolved: (1) excessive basal 0.6 U/h is less likely because TBR drops to 3-4.8% in 02:00-06:00 when IOB has fully decayed and average glucose is near target; (2) residual IOB from daytime corrections with DIA 10h is the primary contributor; (3) Dynamic ISF lag in detecting overnight sensitivity increase is a secondary contributor. Daytime hyperglycemia is unequivocally from absent meal boluses, not basal deficit, because the pattern correlates with meal timing rather than a continuous drift. Afternoon crashes are from IOB stacking of UAM-driven corrections with Dynamic ISF over-amplification as a secondary contributor; the 0.5 U/h basal at 16:00 is the lowest segment and crashes occur even when basal is minimal. The safe action order is: (1) disable SMB during temp targets as an independent safety measure, (2) introduce carb entries with existing CR, (3) after one week of meal bolus data, evaluate Dynamic ISF adjustment factor, (4) after stable meal bolusing, consider ISF time segmentation. Changing dependent parameters together is avoided: the Dynamic ISF adjustment factor and ISF profile should not be changed simultaneously, and basal rates should not be adjusted until meal boluses establish a new baseline.
analysis_steps.evidence: Cross-stage synthesis: overnight TBR 10-18% at 00:00-02:00 dropping to 3-4.8% at 02:00-06:00 supports IOB-driven rather than basal-driven hypoglycemia. Daytime TAR 20-32% correlates with meal timing (09:00-16:00) not continuous basal drift. Afternoon TBR 7.7-15.3% occurs despite 0.5 U/h basal (lowest segment). Aug 13 crash: 172 to 42 on 0.2U correction with UAM Boost 2=35.93 and variable_sens=53.4. Aug 14 crash: 234 to 41 on GLP-1 day with variable_sens=42.5. Aug 15 temp target: 174 to 66 with SMB continuing during target. Zero carb entries across 14 days.
analysis_steps.data_gaps: Carb entries needed to validate CR, ISF, and DIA. Fasting windows needed to confirm basal rates. GLP-1 dose-response quantification needed for safe bolus adjustment on injection days.

strengths: Overall TIR of 86.0% is strong despite the absence of meal boluses, demonstrating that UAM and Dynamic ISF provide substantial automated coverage
Overnight glucose stability is good from 02:00-06:00 with TBR dropping to 3.0-4.8% and average glucose of 99.5-106.0 mg/dL near the 90 mg/dL target
CGM data quality is excellent at 98.7% coverage with only minor gaps, supporting reliable pattern analysis
Basal rate profile is structurally well-segmented with appropriate step-ups for dawn (05:00-08:00) and a protective low segment at 16:00-18:00 (0.5 U/h)
CR segmentation is logically structured with more aggressive ratios during periods of observed higher insulin sensitivity (10.5 g/U at 16:00-20:00)
Max basal (12 U/h) and max IOB (25 U) limits are appropriately set as non-binding safety backstops that do not interfere with automated delivery
issues: Zero carbohydrate entries across the entire 14-day period. All meal coverage is reactive UAM, creating a consistent cycle of unannounced meals producing hyperglycemia (TAR up to 32%), delayed UAM-driven insulin delivery, IOB stacking, and subsequent hypoglycemia (TBR up to 18.5% overnight, 15.3% in evenings)

SMB continues to deliver insulin during user-set temp targets of 135 mg/dL (smb_with_temp_target_enabled=true). On Aug 15, glucose fell from 174 to 66 mg/dL during a temp target period when the user was explicitly requesting reduced insulin delivery

Dynamic ISF adjustment factor of 70% allows effective ISF to drop to approximately 30% of profile, contributing to overcorrection crashes. Observed variable_sens as low as 27.8 mg/dL/U on Aug 21 and 37.9 mg/dL/U on Aug 19. Severe crashes include 172 to 42 mg/dL (Aug 13) and 234 to 41 mg/dL (Aug 14, GLP-1 day)
Glycemic variability is elevated at CV 32.6%, driven by the reactive UAM-only meal coverage pattern and the hyperglycemia-overcorrection cycle
DIA of 10 hours combined with single-segment ISF means residual IOB from afternoon corrections persists into overnight hours, contributing to the 10-18.5% TBR in the 00:00-02:00 window
GLP-1 doses (1.25mg on Aug 14, 17, 20) are recorded as notes but not as structured treatments, preventing automated sensitivity adjustment on injection days

recommendations.title: Begin carbohydrate entries for all meals
recommendations.description: Introduce carbohydrate entries with immediate boluses using the existing CR profile. Start with breakfast and lunch (13.2 g/U at 08:00-16:00) and evening meal (10.5 g/U at 16:00-20:00). This is the single most impactful intervention because it directly addresses the root cause of the primary dysregulation cycle: unannounced meals produce hyperglycemia, UAM responds with delayed insulin, and stacked IOB causes subsequent hypoglycemia. Pre-meal boluses will reduce hyperglycemia peaks, lower total insulin delivered via corrections, and diminish the IOB stacking that drives overnight and afternoon hypoglycemia.

suggested_change.action: Begin entering carbohydrate grams for all meals and delivering immediate boluses using existing CR profile
suggested_change.prebolus: Not yet; start with immediate bolus to establish baseline
suggested_change.observation_period: One week with at least two meals per day entered

recommendations.title: Disable SMB during temporary targets
recommendations.description: Set smb_with_temp_target_enabled to false. The user set six temp targets of 135 mg/dL across the 14-day period, likely for exercise or activity. With SMB enabled during temp targets, the system continues delivering insulin during periods when the user is explicitly requesting reduced insulin delivery. On Aug 15, glucose fell from 174 to 66 mg/dL during a temp target. This is a safety concern that can be addressed independently and immediately, without depending on any other setting change.

recommendations.title: Reduce Dynamic ISF adjustment factor
recommendations.description: Reduce dynamic_isf_adjustment_factor_percent from 70% to 60%. This limits the depth of ISF reduction from approximately 30% of profile to approximately 40% of profile, reducing overcorrection risk during periods of heightened sensitivity (GLP-1 days, activity). The current 70% setting contributed to effective ISF values as low as 27.8 mg/dL/U and severe crashes on Aug 13 (172 to 42) and Aug 14 (234 to 41). This change should be made after one week of meal bolus data is available, because introducing carb entries will change the insulin delivery landscape and may reduce the need for this adjustment.

recommendations.title: Consider ISF time segmentation after meal bolus baseline
recommendations.description: The single ISF segment of 56 mg/dL/U for all 24 hours forces Dynamic ISF to compensate for circadian sensitivity variation. After establishing a stable meal-bolus baseline, consider adding a separate overnight ISF segment (e.g., 00:00-08:00 at 50-52 mg/dL/U) to reflect the higher insulin sensitivity observed during overnight hours. This would reduce the reactive burden on Dynamic ISF and provide more predictable correction behavior. Do not implement this change concurrently with the Dynamic ISF adjustment factor reduction.

suggested_change.suggested_value: Future consideration: separate overnight segment after meal bolus data validates the pattern

profile_recommendation.recommendation: Keep the current profile settings unchanged. The ISF of 56 mg/dL/U, basal rates (0.5-0.8 U/h), CR segments (10.5-13.2 g/U), targets (90-100 mg/dL), and DIA (10 hours) are all structurally reasonable. The observed dysregulation patterns are driven primarily by the absence of meal boluses and secondarily by Dynamic ISF over-amplification and SMB during temp targets, not by incorrect profile values. Changing profile settings before establishing a meal-bolus baseline would be premature and could introduce new instability.
profile_recommendation.rationale: Basal rates produce near-target fasting glucose when IOB has decayed (02:00-06:00, avg 99.5-106.0, TBR 3-4.8%). CR segments are unvalidated but structurally align with observed sensitivity patterns. The single ISF segment is the profile element most likely to benefit from future refinement, but the current value of 56 mg/dL/U is reasonable as a baseline. Dynamic ISF is already providing time-based adjustment. Profile changes should follow, not precede, the introduction of meal boluses.
profile_recommendation.next_check: After one week of carb entries for at least two meals per day, evaluate whether the daytime TAR drops from the current 20-32% toward the target of less than 15%. If TAR remains elevated despite meal boluses, then consider CR adjustment. If overnight TBR remains above 5% after meal boluses reduce daytime IOB, then consider a small basal reduction in the 00:00-05:00 segment.

parameter_decisions.rationale: Average overnight glucose is 93-105 mg/dL near the 90 mg/dL target. TBR is 10-18.5% in the first two hours of the night but drops to 3-4.8% by 02:00-06:00 when IOB has fully decayed. This pattern indicates the hypoglycemia is IOB-driven from daytime corrections (DIA 10h), not excessive basal rate. Changing basal before introducing meal boluses to reduce daytime IOB would be premature.
Glucose is stable at 104.2 mg/dL with TBR 4.8% during this segment. The 0.7 U/h rate provides appropriate coverage for the dawn transition without inducing hypoglycemia.
Glucose is stable at 99.5 mg/dL with TBR 2.5% at 06:00 and 1.3% at 07:00. The 0.8 U/h step-up covers the dawn period effectively. No evidence of basal excess or deficit during this window.

Glucose rises from 132.9 to 148.0 mg/dL during this segment, but the rise coincides with unannounced meal timing and cannot be attributed to basal deficit. The 0.7 U/h rate is a modest reduction from the dawn 0.8 U/h and is structurally appropriate. Do not increase daytime basal without first establishing meal boluses to separate meal-driven from basal-driven glucose rise.

This is the lowest basal segment and is intended as a protective floor during the afternoon insulin sensitivity window. Despite the 0.5 U/h rate, glucose falls from 162.8 to 148.9 mg/dL and TBR rises to 7.7-15.3% by 18:00-19:00. The crashes are driven by correction IOB stacking, not basal excess. Reducing this already-low segment further would risk hyperglycemia if IOB stacking is reduced by meal bolus introduction.

Glucose continues to fall during this segment (124.2 mg/dL at 18:00, TBR 7.7%) but the decline begins in the previous segment and is driven by correction IOB. The 0.6 U/h is a modest step up from the 0.5 U/h floor. Keep until meal boluses establish a new baseline and reduce afternoon IOB.

Glucose stabilizes at 105.4-120.0 mg/dL during this segment with TBR declining from 15.3% at 19:00 to 4.8% by 20:00. The 0.7 U/h rate appears appropriate for the evening transition. The early-evening TBR is a residual effect of afternoon IOB, not the 0.7 U/h basal rate.
No meals are consumed during this overnight window. The 13 g/U value is a reasonable overnight setting. Cannot be validated without carb entries.
No meals are observed during this early morning window. The 11.1 g/U is the most aggressive CR, appropriate for dawn phenomenon insulin resistance. Cannot be validated without carb entries.

This segment covers breakfast and lunch. The 13.2 g/U is a reasonable starting point for daytime meals. Glucose rises during this window but the rise is from unannounced meals with zero bolus insulin, not from incorrect CR. Introduce carb entries with this CR and evaluate after one week.

This is the most aggressive CR segment, consistent with the observed afternoon insulin sensitivity pattern and GLP-1 effect. The 10.5 g/U is structurally appropriate for evening meals. Cannot be validated without carb entries.
This segment covers late evening snacks. The 12.6 g/U is a moderate ratio. Glucose rises modestly during this window (117 to 127.6 mg/dL) but without carb entries, CR validation is not possible.

The single ISF segment of 56 mg/dL/U is a reasonable baseline. Dynamic ISF provides time-based adjustment producing effective values from 27.8 to 124 mg/dL/U. The wide range suggests circadian sensitivity variation exists, but changing the profile ISF before establishing a meal-bolus baseline would be premature. Future ISF segmentation is recommended after meal bolus data validates the sensitivity pattern.

The 90 mg/dL overnight target is appropriate. Average overnight glucose is 93-105 mg/dL, near target. The overnight hypoglycemia is IOB-driven, not target-driven. Raising the target would not address the root cause.
The 100 mg/dL daytime target provides a modest safety buffer. Daytime hyperglycemia is from unannounced meals, not an inappropriate target. The target is appropriate for the current profile.
The transition back to 90 mg/dL at 23:00 is appropriate. Evening glucose averages 105.7 mg/dL at 23:00, above target but not excessively. The TBR of 10.1% is a residual effect of daytime IOB.

DIA of 10 hours means IOB from afternoon corrections persists into overnight hours, contributing to the 00:00-02:00 hypoglycemia pattern. However, U200 diluted insulin may have different kinetics than standard U100, and changing DIA without meal-bolus data to validate insulin duration would be speculative. After meal boluses are established, if overnight hypoglycemia persists despite reduced daytime IOB, DIA reduction to 8-9 hours should be considered.

SMB and UAM must remain enabled. UAM is the sole meal-response mechanism in the current no-bolus workflow. Disabling either would leave meals completely uncovered. Once meal boluses are established, UAM will continue to serve as an essential safety net for under-bolused or missed meals.

smb_with_temp_target_enabled must be changed from true to false. The user set six temp targets of 135 mg/dL across the 14-day period, likely for exercise or activity. With SMB enabled during temp targets, the system continues delivering insulin during periods when the user explicitly requests reduced insulin delivery. On Aug 15, glucose fell from 174 to 66 mg/dL during a temp target period. This is an independent safety change that does not depend on any other setting. All other activation conditions are appropriate: smb_always_enabled=true is needed for UAM-driven meal coverage, and smb_with_cob_enabled=false is appropriate since no carb entries exist.

parameter_decisions.current_value: smb_interval_minutes=3 min; max_smb_basal_minutes=15 min; max_uam_smb_basal_minutes=20 min
parameter_decisions.suggested_value: smb_interval_minutes=3 min; max_smb_basal_minutes=15 min; max_uam_smb_basal_minutes=20 min
parameter_decisions.rationale: The 3-minute SMB interval provides responsive UAM-driven meal coverage. The 15-minute max SMB basal minutes and 20-minute max UAM SMB basal minutes are appropriate for the current basal rates (0.5-0.8 U/h), producing SMB doses of 0.125-0.27 U. These settings are not excessive and should be maintained.

parameter_decisions.parameter: AAPS / max basal and max IOB limits
parameter_decisions.rationale: Both limits are non-binding safety backstops. Highest observed temp basal: 3.6 U/h. Highest observed IOB: 5.935 U. The 12 U/h and 25 U limits do not constrain actual delivery and function as appropriate safety ceilings. No changes are needed.

Dynamic ISF adjustment factor should be reduced from 70% to 60%. The current 70% setting allows effective ISF to drop to approximately 30% of profile (theoretical floor 16.8 mg/dL/U). Observed variable_sens reached 27.8 mg/dL/U, contributing to overcorrection crashes on Aug 13 (172 to 42 mg/dL) and Aug 14 (234 to 41 mg/dL, GLP-1 day). At 60%, the floor rises to approximately 40% of profile (22.4 mg/dL/U theoretical), reducing overcorrection risk while retaining substantial sensitivity adaptation. Autosens remains appropriately disabled since Dynamic ISF is active. This change should be made after one week of meal bolus data confirms the pattern persists under the new workflow.

The 8 mg/dL/5 min min_5m_carbimpact is standard for UAM COB estimation. The 7-hour meal_max_absorption_hours is at the high end of typical ranges and may extend UAM-modeled COB beyond actual meal duration, contributing to phantom IOB. However, changing this setting without carb entries for calibration would be speculative. Once meal boluses are established, if afternoon hypoglycemia persists despite adequate bolusing, reducing meal_max_absorption_hours to 5-6 hours should be considered.

meal_strategy_summary.suggestion: Begin entering carbohydrate grams for all meals and deliver immediate boluses (100% upfront, no prebolus timing yet) using the existing CR profile. Use 13.2 g/U for breakfast and lunch (08:00-16:00), 10.5 g/U for evening meals (16:00-20:00), and 12.6 g/U for late snacks (20:00-00:00). Keep SMB and UAM enabled as a safety net for under-bolused or missed meals, but disable SMB during temporary targets. E-carbs are not yet applicable; establish basic meal bolusing first. Do not use prebolus timing initially; start with immediate bolus to establish a baseline of meal response data before optimizing timing.
meal_strategy_summary.rationale: The absence of carbohydrate entries is the root cause of the primary glycemic dysregulation cycle. All meal coverage is currently reactive UAM, which detects meals only after glucose begins rising, creating a 15-30+ minute insulin delivery lag. This produces daytime hyperglycemia (TAR 20-32%), triggers aggressive UAM-driven corrections, and leads to IOB stacking that causes overnight hypoglycemia (TBR 10-18%) and afternoon crashes (TBR 7-15%). Introducing carb entries with immediate boluses will deliver insulin coincident with meal absorption, reducing hyperglycemia peaks and the subsequent IOB stacking. The existing CR profile is structurally reasonable and should be used as the starting point. One week of meal-bolus data is needed before any CR adjustments can be validated.
meal_strategy_summary.next_observation: After one week of carb entries for at least two meals per day using the existing CR of 13.2 g/U (daytime) and 10.5 g/U (evening), evaluate whether the daytime TAR drops from the current 20-32% toward the target of less than 15%, and whether the afternoon TBR drops from 7.7-15.3% toward less than 5%.

exceptions.pattern: GLP-1 injection days (currently every 3-4 days: Aug 14, 17, 20)
exceptions.suggestion: On GLP-1 injection days, consider reducing meal boluses by 10-20% or setting a temp target of 120-130 mg/dL for 6-8 hours post-injection. The Aug 14 data shows extreme insulin sensitivity (variable_sens dropped to 42.5 mg/dL/U) with a severe crash from 234 to 41 mg/dL. GLP-1 is recorded as a note but not as a structured treatment, so the system cannot automatically adjust. Until GLP-1 effects are better characterized with meal-bolus data, proactive bolus reduction on injection days is a prudent precaution.
exceptions.rationale: GLP-1 receptor agonists increase insulin sensitivity and slow gastric emptying. The three recorded doses correlate with the most severe hypoglycemic events in the dataset. Dynamic ISF detects this sensitivity increase but with a lag, meaning initial bolus and correction doses may be delivered at the pre-GLP-1 ISF before the system adapts.

exceptions.pattern: Activity periods with temp targets of 135 mg/dL
exceptions.suggestion: During activity-related temp targets, disable SMB (smb_with_temp_target_enabled=false, implemented as a permanent setting change) and consider reducing or skipping meal boluses if eating within 1-2 hours of activity. The Aug 15 event shows glucose falling from 174 to 66 mg/dL during a temp target when SMB continued delivering insulin. The temp target of 135 mg/dL signals the user's intent to reduce insulin delivery, but the current settings do not fully respect this intent.
exceptions.rationale: Exercise increases insulin sensitivity and glucose utilization. The temp target raises the glycemic target but does not fully suppress insulin delivery when SMB remains active. Combined with the already-high afternoon insulin sensitivity pattern, this creates a high-risk window for hypoglycemia.

implementation_steps: Step 1 (safety, independent): Disable smb_with_temp_target_enabled. Set to false in AAPS SMB settings. This change is independent of all other settings and addresses the immediate safety concern of SMB delivering insulin during user-requested reduced-insulin periods. Verify that SMB no longer fires during the next temp target.

Step 2 (foundation, 1 week): Begin entering carbohydrate grams for all meals. Start with at least two meals per day (breakfast and lunch) using the existing CR of 13.2 g/U at 08:00-16:00. Deliver 100% immediate bolus with no prebolus timing. No other profile or automation changes during this week. Observe: daytime TAR trend, afternoon TBR trend, and overnight TBR trend. If GLP-1 injection occurs during this week, proactively reduce meal boluses by 10-20%.

Step 3 (evaluate, after 1 week of Step 2): Review the new meal-bolus data. If daytime TAR has dropped below 15% and afternoon TBR has dropped below 5%, the meal-bolus intervention is working. If overnight TBR remains above 5% despite reduced daytime IOB, consider DIA reduction or overnight basal adjustment. If daytime TAR remains above 15% despite meal boluses, consider CR adjustment (e.g., 13.2 to 12.0 g/U).

Step 4 (automation, after Step 3 confirms meal-bolus baseline): Reduce dynamic_isf_adjustment_factor_percent from 70% to 60%. This change should only be made after the meal-bolus baseline is established, because introducing carb entries will change the insulin delivery landscape and may reduce the need for this adjustment. Observe for one additional week before making further changes.

Step 5 (future, after Steps 3-4 are stable): Consider ISF time segmentation. If overnight TBR persists or Dynamic ISF continues to show large circadian swings (variable_sens routinely below 40 or above 80), add a separate overnight ISF segment (e.g., 00:00-08:00 at 50-52 mg/dL/U). Do not implement this concurrently with the Dynamic ISF adjustment factor change. Wait at least one week between automation changes.
education: UAM (Unannounced Meal) detection works by identifying unexpected glucose rises that cannot be explained by current IOB and basal insulin. It creates virtual carbohydrates and delivers insulin accordingly. While UAM is an effective safety net, it is inherently reactive and cannot match the glycemic control of announced meals with pre-bolusing. The 15-30 minute delay between meal onset and UAM response is the primary reason for the daytime hyperglycemia pattern observed in your data.

Dynamic ISF adjusts your insulin sensitivity factor in real time based on observed glucose responses. The 70% adjustment factor means your ISF can vary from approximately 30% to 100% of the profile value (56 mg/dL/U). This is why your effective ISF ranges from about 28 to 56 mg/dL/U. The adjustment is reactive, meaning it detects sensitivity changes after they have begun affecting your glucose. This lag is why periods of rapidly increasing sensitivity (GLP-1 onset, exercise) can still produce hypoglycemia.

DIA (Duration of Insulin Action) of 10 hours means that insulin from a correction bolus at 16:00 is still considered active until 02:00 the next morning. This is why your overnight hypoglycemia clusters in the 00:00-02:00 window. When you introduce meal boluses, the total daily insulin delivery pattern will change, and the overnight IOB burden may decrease naturally.

Temporary targets raise your glucose target for a specified duration. They are typically used for exercise or activity to reduce insulin delivery. However, when SMB is enabled during temp targets, the system may still deliver correction microboluses. The temp target reduces the aggressiveness of insulin delivery but does not completely stop it unless SMB is also disabled during the target.
safety_notes: This is decision-support content only. The user must independently verify every proposed change, make changes one at a time, and monitor glucose closely. TuneMyBG prepares data for review only and does not provide medical advice.

The primary safety concern is SMB continuing to deliver insulin during user-set temporary targets of 135 mg/dL. This undermines the protective intent of the temp target and contributed to a severe drop from 174 to 66 mg/dL on Aug 15. Disable smb_with_temp_target_enabled as the first and most urgent change.

GLP-1 doses (1.25mg) are recorded as notes but not as structured treatments. The system cannot automatically adjust insulin delivery for GLP-1-enhanced sensitivity. On injection days, consider proactive meal bolus reduction and close glucose monitoring, especially in the 4-8 hours post-injection when sensitivity peaks.

The Dynamic ISF adjustment factor of 70% contributed to effective ISF values as low as 27.8 mg/dL/U and severe crashes to 41-42 mg/dL. Reducing this to 60% will limit the depth of ISF reduction. However, this change should be made after establishing a meal-bolus baseline, not before, because the absence of meal boluses is currently the dominant driver of the overcorrection cycle.

Do not change the Dynamic ISF adjustment factor and ISF profile segmentation at the same time. These settings interact: both affect the effective ISF used for correction and meal bolus calculations. Changing them together would make it impossible to determine which change caused any observed effect. Wait at least one week between automation changes.

When introducing carb entries, start with the existing CR values. Do not simultaneously adjust CR, ISF, basal rates, or DIA. The goal of the first week is to establish a clean baseline of meal-bolus response data. Multiple simultaneous changes would confound the evaluation of which setting is working or needs adjustment.

The max IOB of 25 U and max basal of 12 U/h are not causing harm and should remain as safety backstops. Do not reduce them as a way to limit correction insulin; the pattern of overcorrection is driven by Dynamic ISF and UAM timing, not by excessive safety limits.
